## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome are reported to have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual antiepileptic treatments. In a small number of cases, epilepsy can be difficult to treat.

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The cardiologist found a structural abnormality in the patient's heart. They recommend regular check-ups to monitor the condition and ensure it doesn't affect the patient's daily life.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural abnormalities. A few require surgery, while some just need monitoring.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: Our son gains weight slowly compared to his peers, and he eats well without showing signs of discomfort after eating. However, he doesn't seem to put on weight as quickly as other kids his age.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome are reported to have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual antiepileptic treatments. In a small number of cases, epilepsy can be difficult to treat.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a brain-related issue, specifically a tethered cord, which could potentially affect his development. Doctors are keeping a close eye on how he progresses.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have brain-related issues, specifically a tethered cord, which could potentially affect their development.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: Our son experiences feeding difficulties and requires short-term nasogastric tube feeding to supplement oral feeds. Lack of interest in feeding can be significant and long-lasting.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have feeding difficulties, requiring short-term nasogastric tube feeding to supplement oral feeds.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: Our son has scoliosis, and we're working with physical therapy to help improve his posture and reduce the curvature of his spine.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have scoliosis.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: Our son experiences tooth sensitivity when eating cold foods like ice cream or cold yogurt.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome experience tooth sensitivity.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: Our son needs extra help in school, though most go to a mainstream primary school. The extra demands of mainstream secondary school may prove too challenging, and he may transfer to special schooling or remain in mainstream schools with Educational Health Care Plans (EHCP).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome need extra help in school, though most go to a mainstream primary school.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: Our son has behavioral differences such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), or anxiety. Medication(s) may be appropriate in some circumstances.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have behavioral differences, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), or anxiety.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: Our son has scoliosis, and we're working with physical therapy to help improve his posture and reduce the curvature of his spine.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have scoliosis.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Regular dental check-ups: Our son experiences tooth sensitivity when eating cold foods like ice cream or cold yogurt.
b) Regular hearing reviews to age 5: Even if earlier reviews give a clear response, regular hearing reviews to age 5 are recommended.
c) Eyesight (ophthalmology) review: Regular eye checks are recommended to monitor vision.
d) Check position of testes in boys: Regular examination of the testes position is advised.
e) Consider a palate review: Particularly if there are feeding difficulties or speech concerns.
f) Referral for a cardiac review (including echo and ECG): Following diagnosis, a cardiac review is recommended.
g) If nothing is found (or already done) this does not need to be repeated.
h) Consider a skeletal review (X-ray of the wrist (to determine bone age), hip, spine and skull): Children following diagnosis should undergo a skeletal review.
i) Any concerns around asymmetric hip creases in infancy and/or asymmetric or painful gait should prompt medical review.
j) Consider review and investigation for tethered cord (MRI) where clinical concerns arise on an individual basis (especially if sacral dimple is present).
k) Monitor growth velocity: If height is below the 2nd centile, refer for endocrine investigations on an individual basis and within context of familial heights.
l) Consider physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy and behavioural therapy: Regular assessments and interventions are recommended based on the patient's needs.
